description:
Folk story/mythology of red beans on Winter Solstice. 

Traditions of red bean porridge can be traced back to 1046 BC to the Zhou Dynasty. The story goes the young son of Gong Gong hated red beans and died on Winter Solstice. His son turned into a plague spirit. To ward off the disease spreading spirit, people began to put out and scatter red bean around their homes. 

There are 3 different types of Dongji depending on the it's date: Aedongji, Jungdongji and Nodongji. 
Korea used to celebrate Winter Solstice as their new year until 1309 when Goryeo switched to the Shoushi Calendar during Yuan Dynasty. During Winter Solstice it was believed that Koreans turned a year older on Dongji after eating a bowl of patjuk.

Calendars and quilted socks were given as gifts to promote good luck.

description:
동지 (Dongji) - Winter Solstice is this Monday (Dec 21). A very particular type of winter solstice, specifically called 애동지 (Ae Dongji). 

On winter solstice, family would gather to make and eat red bean porridge known as 팥죽 (patjuk). But this year, we won't cook and eat the red bean porridge because its an ae-dongji 애동지 - its believed that harm can come to children. Meaning that this winter solstice eating patjuk can leave children unprotected. 

To kinda further explain, one teacher from Korea said that because red bean porridge is used for its exorcism  abilities - Samshin 삼신할매 (goddess of childbirth, and protector of children) CANT come and protect the children during this time if the porridge is consumed or used. 

On winter solstice, I normally prepare a spread of numerous offerings along with bowls of red bean porridge. Each room in the home will also have a bowl placed to cleanse the  home. In older times doors are marked, walls and fences are splattered with the red bean porridge to drive out negative spirits.

Neighbors and villagers would gather in communal exorcism ritual, driving out these negative forces from their homes and village. 

But this year being special, and as a mom with young children I wont be setting up offerings or doing any folk ritual in observance to 애동지.

description:
Do you know the story of Korea's last Queen, Empress Myeongseong - Queen Min. ⁣⁣
She came from a powerful clan that had birthed previous Queens. But by the time she was a child, her clan had fallen and she was orphaned. At age 16, she married Gojong. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Her authority as Queen was shaken when the Kings consort birthed a son while Queen Min was childless. Then 20, she finally became pregnant and birthed a son. The baby was ill and needed treatment but passed away. ⁣⁣
She hired shamans and brought mudangs into the palace to find the root cause of her son's untimely passing. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Queen Min association and relationship with mudangs ran deep. She would often sponsor kut 굿 ceremony/ritual. Even at one point, she adopted a mudang as her daughter, a princess. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
I been researching and digging into the Mudang princess. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Queen Min was assassinated by Korean and Japanese assassins due to her opposition against Japanese. They stormed into the Queens quarter, assaulting the women. The assassin took body, burned it and scattered her ashes. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Her marriage with the King was rocky and political, but over time they grew deep love. The King ordered to search for her body, and a funeral was held. He built wooden horses to escort the nation's beloved Queen to the afterworld. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
[In my research, they say that no one really knew what Queen Min looked like, and a portrait was drawn based on their presumptions of what she looked like. Only very few people knew the identity of Queen Min, even her assassin had a hard time]⁣
⁣
⁣⁣
⁣
Side note: alot of details were omitted due to the extreme violence. I did not want to trigger anyone. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Inspired by my conversation with @leedoyun . Thank you. ⁣

Sunday Shout out! 😘

There are no words for the amount of love and respect I have for Jenn. When I first met her, I was unsure of my path. Growing up between worlds, in this case Korean and not, makes the boundaries unclear. 

Jenn assured me feeling that way was normal, and that I was welcome just as anybody else in our ancestor's space. She told me how my ancestors were calling out to me if we were connecting. 

She was 100% correct. 

After our reading together, my body woke me up from a dream. In my dream, I was dancing in a folk village. It was similar to the Folk Village we visited when I was a child. 

The dirt streets were filled with people, my ancestors, dancing and singing. As my dream body moved to the music, my physical body moved in this reality. As it sat up, my consciousness snapped back and I opened my eyes. 

I was sitting up in bed, arms outstretched in front of me, frozen in the ribbon like pattern I was recreating with them. I immediately messaged @shaman.mudang and told her about it, how I felt so much joy in that moment. 

I can still feel it two years later....

Her dedication to the craft makes her a fountain of knowledge. Her love for her community is evident in the smallest of tasks she accomplishes. The love and respect she has for the old ways is beyond admirable. 

And everything she does clearly comes from her heart. 

I am honored to have such a wonderful person in my life. Forever Grateful to do this thing called life with her. Thank you for all you've supported me through. 🙏🏼

description:
There are many types of paintings depicting gods in various styles. If you look closely and observe the symbolism, it tells a story. ⁣
⁣
In these shamanic portraits of Sanshin 산신 god of mountain, the deity is holding a white feathered fan. A symbol noting back to the mythology of Danggun (the grandson of Heavens). ⁣
White feather fans are usually connected to the white crane. The crane is symbolic for nobility, emblem rank for government officials. A longevity symbol known for its regal, integrity and its sagacity wisdom.  The white crane is a spiritual and holy symbol for its magic and magical essence of longevity. ⁣
When Sanshin is shown with a white feather fan, its referring to Sanshin authority to command the wind. Sanshin is god of mountain, the earth and guardian of all within. Sanshin authority ties back to the myth of Danggun (the grandson of Heavens- Hwanin). Hwanung (Danggun father) descended from the Heavens with the god of rain, wind and cloud under his command. ⁣
Danggun transformed and turned into Sanshin.⁣
⁣
Some times feathers are also used as ritual tools during ceremony, or used as altar items. Hats are adorned with feathers referring to the mudang shaman ability of flight, traveling within the realms of the upper, middle and lower. ⁣
⁣
⁣
Check out this yeo-sanshin, the female mountain god. ⁣The flowing fabric drawn behind her - another indicator of flight. ⁣
⁣
⁣

July 17th was CHOBOK 초북. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Sambok 삼북 are 3 days thats considered the hottest during the year. When the yin energy falls and yang energy rises. ⁣⁣
•Chobok 초북 is the 1st hottest day⁣⁣
•Jungbok 중북 2nd hottest day⁣⁣
•Malbok 말북 3rd hottest day.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
The philosophy and concept of Sambok goes back to the Qing dynasty. ⁣⁣
⁣For villages, sambok is welcomed because the heat made the rice grow quickly. ⁣⁣
 ⁣⁣
Traditional foods like gingseng chicken soup is eaten on this day, to promote food health. Ginseng helps fill in lacking nutrition, revitalizing our soul and spirit.⁣⁣
In older times dog meat soup was consumed due to lack of metal energy. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Going on picnics, swimming in rivers, eating watermelons, melons or drinking water from natural wells are all part of the tradition of the Sambok rituals. ⁣⁣
We celebrate this traditions by  honoring our ancestors. ⁣
⁣
❤🙇‍♀️💛 ⁣

To learn more about the story of these young women and girls, and the ways that their experiences as well as imperial violence continue to shape public art across the globe, be sure to watch "When it's not okay to take down a statue," in our Monumental Women series.

I am thrilled to announce that my new film installation 'Four Months, Four Million Light Years' (2020) is part of the 11th Berlin Biennale, opening today
 
‘Four Months, Four Million Light Years’ (2020) is a shamanic healing journey addressing the colonial narratives behind interracial and intercountry adoption, specifically the historical relations between The Netherlands and Korea. The film takes the colonial print ‘Een Schaman ofte Duyvel-Priester’ (Shaman or Devil’s Priest from the Tungus) (1692) by the Dutchman Nicolaes Witsen as the starting point for a spiritual journey through time. The seventeenth-century print is the first Western depiction of a shaman. It marks the beginning of a long history of racialized and infantilizing descriptions of Asian people by white Europeans. The caricature image was later used by missionaries to marginalize shamanism.

‘Four Months, Four Million Light Years’ time-travels from contemporary Dutch society to the participation of 3,418 Dutch soldiers in the deadly Korean War (1950–1953) to early Dutch colonial descriptions of Asian people. The artist herself is an adoptee from Korea and grew up in The Netherlands. In The Netherlands alone around 40,000 people have been adopted from the Global South to the Global North, often through child trafficking and with falsified documents. The “four months” of the title refer to the time it took to make a Korean child available for the lucrative interracial adoption industry that flourished after the Korean War, an industry that continues to live off the same colonial imagery from 300 years ago. 

In the room, textile banners surround the video projection. Here, shamanic poems, songs and visions invoke the ancestors for support. The work is an homage to those who have been cut off from their mothers, fathers, family, ancestors, land, culture and spirits.

Co-produced by the @kunstenfestivaldesarts

description:
Happy Earth Day 🌎⁣
⁣
We celebrate and gives thanks to the Earth for all her bounty and blessings. ⁣
There are many things we can do to contribute, whenever we go to beaches, walk along mountain roads or hiking if there is garbage littered...my family picks it up. ⁣
⁣
I can sit here all day next to this waterfall. If this was Korea, these pools of cascading waters are the perfect spot for 선녀 Heavenly Fairy Maidens. Pools of water that collects by a waterfall are often called 선녀 탕. ⁣

description:
Great Full Moon 대보름 Offering Preparations. 

This Full moon is known as 대보름 DaeBoreum which means the Great Full Moon. Its the last day of celebration for the Lunar New Year festival.

Specific offerings to prepare for this celebration. 보름 나물 boreum-namul  translates to full moon vegetables which refers to dried vegetables from previous harvest. The dried vegetables are individually prepared. 

오곡밥 Ogok bap known as 5 grain rice is made of glutinous rice mixed with different beans and grains from previous harvest. 

There are mythology stories and various folk beliefs that are  associated with these dish, that I will share later. These offerings are made to the Heavens, spirits and ancestors to petition for bountiful harvest that year. 

There are several festive activities to do to celebrate the Great Full Moon of the Lunar New Year like the burning of the Moon house, charcoal in a tin car, lantern lighting, drinking specialized liquor, selling your 'heat', etc. 

Wishing everyone an amazing Great Full Moon, and Lantern festival. ✨🏮

Last year, we were able to capture a heartbreaking and inspirational story of Ji-Hwan, who, despite his own financial struggles raising his daughter on his own, was running an organization to help other single fathers in Korea. If you haven’t seen that video yet, you should watch it first to understand the context (Find ""Being a Single Father in Korea"" on our channel (link in bio)). He really wanted to see us again and show us how he used the money to help fellow single fathers. If you still want to donate, you can visit his crowdfunding page (You can find the link in our TAKE ACTION / GIVE Story Highlight). Being a single parent is extremely difficult. ⁣

description:
Today we are cleaning up both our yards, tidying up. Planning out, mapping out where the raised garden beds will be. 

This year planting some special seeds Korean white dandelions, bottle gourds, joseon pumpkin ❤

I grew with my maternal grandparents (before my parents divorce) and we spent everyday in the community garden. My grandparents along with other immigrant elders turned a local dump into a thriving natural farming community in the 90s - in Flushing.

In the summer I make my rounds around the community garden exchanging our garden goods with the others. I grew up digging in the soil, playing in a field of cosmos under the care of the community elders. 

My grandma and I would push our little cart. And sell vegetables on the street sidewalks of Flushing - right by Union street and Roosevelt. 

I reunited with grandma when I was about 16, she was already in the hospital. Everday I stopped by to massage her, and reposition her to prevent sores on her body. Later she was moved to another facility. She passed away, but my mother didn't tell. It wasn't until a week after her funeral did I learn about her passing. 

I was upset and angry at my mom for robbing that opportunity to say goodbye and pay my respects.  And so I return back to the earth, digging in her soul as an act and tribute to my grandmother. I miss her, but she is with me as my ancestral guide and spirit - guiding me on this path as a spiritworker. 

I share that with my children as we explore the miracles of growing our food and our soul.

description:
The earliest landscape painting unearthed from the Korean peninsula revealed (near Pyongyang) Korea's own Goddess of love, beauty, and immortality. ⁣
⁣
The goddess is known as So wang-mo 소왕모, Fairy Queen of the Western Sea, Fairy Peach and even Seonyeo.  She grows a peach tree on a mountain top in her Jade palace besides Jasper Lake.  The tree leaves bud, growing every 3,000 years and taking another 3,000 years for the peach to ripen. ⁣
⁣
When the goddess isn't painted, she's symbolized by her peaches, the fruit of immortality. ⁣
⁣
소왕모 is also known as the Queen Mother of the West, and in the Chinese culture, she is known as Xi Wangmu with Daoist orgins, known as the wife of the Jade Emperor. ⁣
The 3rd son of King Sejong in 1447, dreamt of the peach orchard of 소왕모. A painter was summoned to create the dream vision for the Prince drawn on silk. ⁣
⁣
There are famous Korean art pieces showcasing the "Banquet of Sowangmo (XiWangmu)" from the Joseon Dynasty. ⁣
⁣
The 2nd picture shows 소왕모 with her maiden helper from the Goguryeo Kingdom period, as noted by the National Museum of Korea.⁣

description:
This may be triggering to some. This story contains murder and family violence. ⁣
⁣
In a rural village, less than an hour outside of Seoul there lived a elderly woman. She was the village mudang, a bosal (a bodhisattva). ⁣Her grandmother before her, was a great manshin of her village as well.

Everyone would come to her for advice. Villagers were often poor and bartered goods like chickens, cows, sacks of rice, sugar, and salt in exchange for the mudangs work. ⁣
She was a strict and dedicated woman devoting her life to the gods and Buddha. She was able to build a small temple for her community,  becoming the shrine keeper. ⁣
She was blessed with many children, and grandchildren but no one wanted to follow in grandma's footsteps. ⁣
For years grandma would try to pass on and teach one of her children, but they all refused and was scared. ⁣
As time grew grandma aged and she worried relentlessly about passing the family gods, ancestral deities and guardian spirits.⁣
Post Korean war, many struggle to survive and times were incredibly difficult. Her oldest son has been pestering his parents to sell the land of the shrine and temple. Many arguments and the parents firmly refused, and relationship was rocky.
⁣
While his father was fetching water from their own private well, he pushed his father down into it. He dragged his mother and locked her in the shrine with no food and water. The mudang grandmother fought relentlessly and her last words was - that Sanshin grandfather (god of the mountain) and his tiger will come for him. ⁣
⁣
3 days later, in a horrific accident the oldest son passed away. News spread like willdfire in the village, and the land was deemed cursed from all the horrors that unfolded. ⁣
Developers came, bought out the land and decided to bulldoze and tear down the shrines. They erect tall apartments buildings but workers began to get sick or die from accidents. Many contractors were scared and buildings took a long time to complete. ⁣
Once residents started to move in, many would get sick or pass away from freak incidents. Rumors started to circulate that the land was haunted by the mudang and her gods. ⁣
⁣
⁣
Continued in the next post.⁣

description:
Korea had many names and titles, through history. "The land of the morning calm" is an English nickname created and popularized by Percival Lowell in 1885.

Korea had many names...but once was known as "the land of leopards". 
Leopards roamed the Korean peninsula, even outnumbered the tigers. Leopards were feared and source of many folk stories. Even in folk paintings and art, leopards are drawn comically and paired with magpies. Leopards were hunted to extinction during the Occupation and were even referred as the Korean leopard. 

Pictured is my 산신 신복 (Sanshin sinbok) ceremonial spirit regalia of the Mountain god with Leopard motifs.

One of the special dishes prepared is 약밥 yak-bap translate to medicinal rice for its use of honey. Honey is known for its medicinal qualities and referred to as 약 yak medicine in older times. 

약밥 history is recorded in Samguk Yusa, and tied to a story how a crow saved a Silla King when the Queen was plotting his death. 

Rituals and rites in the winter season used 약밥 as offerings in place of fruit when its out of season. 

I pour my heart into making this 약밥 offering, to give my gratitude to the Heavens, spirits and ancestors. 

Food is medicine.

description:
Dismantling altar and taking down the shrine. 
I only have a small tiny window to take down my shrine and move into a new location. 
We can't move out shrines whenever we want. Spirit mom grabbed the dates (27th & 28th) for me.
Waited past midnight to start handling all my altar items, tools, ritual clothing, weapons, etc.

Tomorrow we wrap the mural and with the most gentle intentions, when we move it. Later on, I plan to have a custom built altar to fit the new space. 
We pushed the moving date for this week, and now scrambling to get things done. 

Later, spirit mom will come when the shrine room 신당 is ready and we need to perform a few necessary rituals. 
•A house GOSA (blessing ritual) appealing to the house spirits (gasin 가신) along with the Earth goddess (jishin 지신) or teoju (local site spirit). 
•Cleansing, purification of my shrineroom, altar and mural to place and seat my gods and ancestral deities. 

I wont be taking any clients for the time being, while i take some time to settle down my gods and the family. I promise, be back soon. Thanks for understanding. 

• • • • • • •

Pictures of a few items. 

 1: shrine and altar room with my taenghwa 턍화  mural in the room center.
2. Shoes belonging to my child spirits, our child god which sometime requires more attention and CANDY. 
3. Part of the gods regalia, the hat of daegam 대감 god of fortune/prosperity/business. 
4. The hat for Sanshin 산신, see the feathers on each side, faux crane feathers. The symbolism goes back to the Danggun mythology, a nod to the ability to control the power of the winds. Also symbolic for flight of the mudangs spirit during trance possession. 

I have so many other things  but I am completely exhausted.

description:
Time is precious to everyone. 
Becareful with who you give your time to. As a mom with kids my time is limited and valuable to me. 

A few months ago, I came across someone working on their path as a neoshaman. We started to chat and had good conversations. We were so deep in our conversations that we chatted until the sun rose the next morning for 6-7 hours straight. Woah. 

She wanted to write a paper about her initiation, and even ask me to conduct a lecture or something for her university. She ask for my personal address to send candy or offering as a token of gratitude. I gave her my address without thinking...only later to find out I was lied to. 
Why I dont give out my personal information - Thanks Sara!! Always a bad apple to spoil the rest. 

Next thing I know, she is part of some smearing campaign about me. In a private Facebook group, they continue their slander. 

I've messaged the person directly only to be blocked, when confronting them. I'm not a person of conflict, matter of fact... I run and flee from it. But finally decided to address this after all  these months. I'm tired of being cornered and feeling like I did some thing wrong when clearly - I am not the problem. 

Yes, Sara . Because I wasn't able to say it after all this time. Stop with the BS. And if you choose to carry on, and spend more time spewing it then that is your prerogative. 

You know what they say, when someone accuses you of doing something - its usually they're the ones doing it. A sign that they are in pain, and wishing healing and recovery.

"When you know who you are--you know what you deserve. Your boundaries are clear and you are also responsible enough to police your own intentions. You know why you do what you do and your integrity is such, that you are willing to curtail behaviors that compromise your recovery as well as the recovery of others." L. Romano

description:
I said no, no, no. 

A university in France reached out. They wanted me to speak and teach their Korean studies class about shamanism. Until they wanted my labor for free. They said they didn't have funding in their budget for my time and labor. I declined. 

 I was supposed to teach a winter course on Korean art, literature and culture studies sharing our shamanism. Until it was time to review the budget, they didn't want to compensate for my time/labor. Apparently, being a Christian school, viewed this overseas course as a missionary trip. That's a big no.

I said no to everything. 
I always wanted to teach, thought about going back to school to teach. 

A blessing in disguise. 
Truthfully, I felt conflicted. 
I wanted to teach Korean diaspora, not white Christian students. 

This experience helped me realign my goals and thoughts. I don't need to teach at academic institutions to be valid. After working with a few professors and researchers, these academic spaces are not open to learning, but their interest is in reinforcing their narratives. 

When the researcher submitted their work on my story as a Korean American mudang, it was edited because my story and experience was too fringe. My story was a bit wild to be accepted, and edited to fit the conservative narrative. 

This year I've been saying no. 
No - to things that's doesn't align with me. 
No - to people that doesn't value me
No - to friends who weren't

I say no so I can make room for FUCK YES! 
Saying no, made space for so much more.

description:
Korean Shamanism is political. ⁣
Its been battered, shaped and molded by governing policies for centuries. ⁣
⁣
Shamans were called in to perform rituals and ceremonies in palaces by Kings and Queens. Performing rituals like rain rites, national security, for the country and used as political instruments. 
⁣
In the 1980s, a group of college student banded together to put on a public performance as protest. ⁣
⁣
Madang Kut was adapted as an artful form of political protest, that touched upon the hearts of those who watched.⁣
Performed by students, used as a vechile to deliver a STRONG message of hope and resistance. ⁣
⁣
⁣
As I learn more deeply about our sacred spiritual traditions, couldn't just bypass and dismiss the political histories that has colored our practice, shaping our history and the korean mindset. ⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣pictured: holding a fan and bell rattle, mid jump and mid air, dressed in ceremonial regalia called sinbok 신북 or ui-dae 의대. Jumping to invoke and call down the spirits in a kut ceremony. 
⁣
⁣⁣

description:
KUT 굿 is a Korean shamanic ceremony and ritual, often involving grand and elaborate altars, abundant offerings, paper goods, the descent and trance possession of the gods and the spirits of the ancestors. Listed below are some of the kuts that is commonly performed. 

▪︎재수굿 Jesu-kut, a ceremony to bring prosperity, luck and abundance. The god of wealth, fortune and business 대감 Daegam is important in this type of ritual, and require meat offerings to Daegam. Mostly performed for businesses, to bring in luck and prosperity. 
▪︎병굿 byeong-kut, ceremony to aid in sickness and disease. The gods of longevity,  medicine, the General and their officers also play crucial roles.
▪︎49제  is a Buddhist inspired ritual involving the spirit/soul of the recently departed. After 49 days of their death, this ritual helps aid and washing of spirits impurities to enter the spirit world. 
▪︎진옥이 굿 jinogwi-kut, this ceremony is meant to guide the spirit and soul of the deceased that hasn't departed. Spirits that missed their chance and now stuck here, wandering and hungry ghosts. Helping release grievances, han and the washing of the spirit. After the spirit is guided back, we unveil ritual tools that reveal reincarnation. Sometimes we can see imprint of a bird, or the body of a dog, prints of a bear, etc that hints on their reincarnation.

 There are too many types of kut ceremony within our traditions. These are just some of the kut ceremony that my lineage actively performs here in the US.

description:
Korean Astrology. 
What is SAJU? 

Rooted from Chinese Bazi astrology.
The astrology uses philosophy of interpreting elemental yin/yang forces. This astrology system is centered and mainly focused on ONE PLANET.
(Take a guess?)

Our ancestors were great scholars of the nights sky, observing the heavens, the stars and the planets. Creating star charts and maps - one the oldest representation of our stars. 

Building the oldest observatory in Asia - the 선덕여왕 Cheomseondae means the star gazing tower. Built in the 7th C during Silla's first reigning female monarch Queen Seondeok. 
*(There is also a drama made about her life, one of my faves). 

Saju is all based on the planetary movement of JUPITER, and the elements corresponds to the position of this planet as it revolves. The elements also represent different planets. 

This system is used in China, Korea, Japan Vietnam and many other Asian countries.

description:
Hide your shoes!

My grandfather taught me alot about folk traditions through his stories. Night before Lunar New Year, you must hide your shoes - putting it away. A misbehaving spirit will come and bring calamity and ill fortune by trying on your shoes and taking it. 

Baskets and sieves were hung up by the entrys and doorways. A spirit will become distracted and mesmerized by the holes in the basket - enchanted, it be there counting the holes till sunrise. A spirit boobytrap of sorts.

Later on through researching I read that these misbehaving spirits are called 야광귀 ya-gwanggi. (Encyclopedia of Korean Folk Culture). 
Hair was collected and burned (spirits really dislike the smell of burnt hair.) The ashes are sprinkled by the front and doorway of the home to repel. 

Pictured is colorful children shoes made in the traditional Korean style. These shoes are on my altar for my child spirits, these shoes are just so cute.

description:
The flag of 고려 Goryeo or Koryo, the Korean kingdom founded in 918.⁣⁣
Goryeo period was known for the Golden Age for Buddhism, achieving the highest influence. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
In the text 'History of the Koryo' a number of references are made about the shaman. Its the official record for the history of the Koryo period. Many occasions the King gathered shamans, having them pray and perform rain rituals. ⁣⁣
One account states that a horse (expensive, only reserved for rich top rank officials) was given as payment for a ceremony. Shaman were not tax-exempt and required to pay taxes in rolls of hemp cloth. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣

description:
Cheo-yong 처용, The Home guardian against illness and disease. ⁣
⁣
One story says King Heongang 49th King of Silla (9th Century) went to pray at the shrine to the Dragon King of the Eastern sea. Pleased with the Kings tribute the Dragon king ordered his 7 sons to shamanically dance and sing songs. One of his sons stayed behind, to serve the royal as a shaman. ⁣The king arranged for Cheo-yong to marry a beautiful woman as his wife. ⁣
⁣
The god of smallpox plague Yeoksin heard about Cheo-yong wife and desired her. One account says Yeoksin shapeshifted and Cheoyong found them together in bed. Cheoyong began to sing poetically. ⁣
⁣
As translated by Peter Lee in the Analogy of Korean Poetry, a verse in the Song of Cheoyong - "having caroused far in the night. In the moonlight capital I return home and in my bed, Behold 4 legs. Two have been mine, whose the other two? Two have been mine, but no no they are taken". ⁣
⁣
Most ancient stories say the god of plague was impressed by Cheoyong song. Yeoksin surrendered and swore never to enter the home where Cheoyong resides. ⁣
⁣
Thus Cheoyong became defied as a gate god, or door god munsin 문신. Usually on the door frame, a picture of Cheoyong is hung as a form of a talisman/amulet accompanied by a bundle of thorny castor oil stems. Used to deter negativity and have exorcism properties. ⁣
⁣
The song and dance of Cheoyong called Cheoyongmu is one of the oldest court ritual designated as UNESCO Cultural Heritage. ⁣
The dancers features red masks (dispel evil) and colored robes associated with the 4 cardinal direction with the center (yellow), red (south), white (west), black (north) and blue (east). ⁣
⁣
⁣⁣
Late Koryo period different version of  Cheoyong songs appeared serving as a basis for ritual exorcism, chasing away the Plague god. ⁣
⁣ ⁣

REPOST 
from @wildbodysomatics 🌌 

Recent calls from multiple BIPOC lead networks and individuals within healing justice work have been powerfully naming the harm that can be done when someone is practicing without training, lineage, and accountability. For white practitioners in particular this is a way we often continue enacting extractive and apppropriative colonial dynamics within healing and wellness communities. ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
Asking about someone’s training is less about having specific certifications and more about practitioners knowing our own nervous systems and embodying our values- or knowing when we have stopped doing these things bc we are human and it happens all the time- and having ways to bring ourselves back to presence and connection. For white folks in particular it is about unlearning urgency and domination. ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
These are not all my original ideas, I have only assembled them. The concept of lineage is deeply rooted in healing justice. Let this be a moment to really listen to what that means in practice.

Some questions you might ask: ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
Does this person have the capacity to ground and resource (or regulate if that’s your language)? How do you feel in your body when you are with them? (An initial consult or the first session is a great way to check this out). ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
How have they trained to do this work? Have they personally taken part in the modality they are offering? How many years have they been in practice before holding space for others? (A minimum of 5 years is a good start) Do they have mentors, teachers, others who offer guidance and support in their work? ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
What lineages do they practice in? What are their relationships to these lineages? to their teachers, the cultural context of the teachings, are they in a practice of being in right relationship to this lineage?(Paying reparations, acknowledging where practices come from)⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
Who are their communities and who are they accountable to? Can you talk to someone who has worked with them? Is there a demonstration of humility in how they approach their work? ⁣⁣⁣Does this person have a process in place for addressing harm and accountability if necessary?

description:
What is a dolmen? ⁣
They are stone tombs, altars and or memorials built with side walls supporting a flat stone on top. They were built sometime during the Neolithic period (1000 BCE) and some later. ⁣
⁣
In Korea, they are called "goindol" which literally means propped stone.⁣
Some dolmens contains remains of high status individuals, buried with all their bronze goods of daggers, bells, swords, pots, etc. ⁣
⁣
Scholars say that some of those buried in the Dolmens belonged to powerful tribal chiefs and/or shamans. One historian says the side stone walls represents Earth, while the top stone slab represents the sky (Heavens). People believed their chieftains souls resided between where Heaven and Earth met. ⁣
⁣
Another nickname for Korea is the Kingdom of Dolmens. 
40% of the worlds doleman are concentrated just in Korea with over 30,000 plus more found. Most Dolmens in urbanized areas were destroyed for development, and not protected.⁣
⁣
⁣
• • • • •⁣
⁣
Dictionary.com ⁣
defines dolmens as chiefly being found in France and Britain. (Being colonizers have its perks)⁣
Dolmens are found throughout the world, NOT chiefly found in France or Britain. ⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣

description:
개양 할미 Gaeyang Halmi⁣
⁣
is the Ocean goddess, ruler of the West sea (Yellow Sea) - indigenous to Korea. Gaeyang Halmi ruled the sea with her 8 daughters. ⁣⁣⁣
소성당 (Suseongdang)the shamanic shrine located in Buan, Jeolla-bukdo. ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
Its said that 개양 할미 was the protective sea goddess that provided safe passage and the protection for the fisherman. The coastal western sea is known for its turbulent and choppy waters, and the goddess is worshipped for her ability control the sea and the winds that affects the currents. ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
Most of her daughters - except the youngest were married and were sent away to other islands and provinces. The goddess is said to be so big and massive that she travels the sea by walking on wooden shoes, controlling the depths of the oceans by filling up the deepest parts.⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
The villagers and shamans still conduct their yearly ritual to the Geayang Halmi Goddess.  Its said and believed that the goddess came from the sea through a dragon cave nearby the shrine [pic 2]. The dragon cave is believed to have 24 hyeol energy centers, its inaccessible due to the rising waters. ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
⁣
⁣
More so than often the ocean gods and deities are depicted as males. Goddess of the Ocean and the sea arent as well known. ⁣
 Spirit mom took us to this shrine, explicitly explaining the importance of this goddess. ⁣⁣⁣
I was very fortunate to have visited this sacred place and making a connection. I still clearly remember the visions I had while in ritual at the shrine. ⁣⁣⁣

노무편 Nomupyeon (Old Shaman) is the earliest written mention of the 무당 mudang (shaman) in Korean text. ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
Written by 이규보 Yi Gyobo a Confucian scholar during the Goryeo dynasty. The poem he wrote expressed his delighted joy when the neighborhood  shaman was expelled, and clearly shows - how much Confucianism despised shamanism. ⁣
One part, Yi marvelled at⁣⁣ "how is she able to live this long". ⁣⁣⁣
⁣
Yi's poem, gives detailed discussion of the shamanic activities, views and attitudes of the people towards shamanism. A crucial piece of evidence that gives detailed accounts of the shaman mudang activities. ⁣⁣⁣

description:
In the lunar month of July, a few important sacred holidays  coming up. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Chilseok day falls on the 7th day of the 7th lunar month. Its a day of celebration performed by mudangs, villagers and the community. ⁣⁣
•Celebration includes the mythical story of two lovers separated by the milky way. ⁣
•Women praying to the goddess for more beautiful embroidery needlework. ⁣⁣
•Rituals to encourage crops and field to grow⁣⁣
•Most importantly, its a day to pay respect and reverance to Chilseong, the 7 stars of the Ursa Major Big Dipper constellation. I've written about this ritual every year when we perform it. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
 ⁣⁣
Later on we celebrate our version of 'All Souls Day' similar to the Mexican festival of 'Dias de Meurtes'. When the gates of the spirit world open, and we commemorate the dead, the spirits and our ancestors. A ritual of to purify the village is perform to protect the community from calamities. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Its very important folk holiday and said to be on the verge of extinction and no longer practiced as a community.
⁣⁣Looking forward to celebrating these deeply rooted traditions. Stay tuned, will share more information as the days comes. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣

description:
A man named 손동지 Son Dongji was exile to Jejudo island, and due to a windstorm his boat crashed. He ended up washed up on the shores of 호동 Hodong village which translates to Tiger Place. 

The villagers was constantly preyed and attacked by the stalking tigers. The villagers decided to flee to the nearby 모도 Modo Island on a raft/boat, unknowingly leaving behind 뽕 할머니 Grandmother Ppong. 

Everyday Ppong Grandmother prayed to the 용왕님 (Yongwang) Dragon King of the Sea in hopes to reunite with her family and villagers. One day Yongwang appeared in her dreams, told her  rainbow 🌈 will fall over the sea, to guide her across to 모도 Modo Island. 
The next day Grandmother Ppong went to the sea, prayed to the Dragon King and  bridge with a rainbow appeared. 

When a bridge with rainbow above appeared, the villagers of Modo grabbed their gongs and percussion - banging on it, to find Grandmother Ppong. They found that she collapsed, and her last words was "나의 기도로 바닷길 열려 너희들을 만났으니 이젠 한이 없다". "Through my prayers, I was able to open the sea road and meet you, I have no more han (deep rooted grievances)" 

Grandmother Ppong ascended to the heavens became a god called 영등 Yeongdeung (god sea and wind). The villagers renamed the village from 호동 Hodong to 회동 Hoedong. 
Every year  annually when the sea bridge appear villagers from both Modo and Hoedong, cross over to meet while they collect seafood, gifts from the sea. 
Its become a sacred place where people pray for fishermans, abundance from the sea and their own wishes. 
This is one of the many stories of Korea's costal island where the myths are still alive and told. Jindo Island historically been used as a refuge during the Mongol invasion, well known for their special dog breeds called Jindo dog (진돗개). 
 
In 1975, a French ambassador Pierre Landy calls Jindo sea parting as the Korean moses miracle referring to the biblical parting of the Red Sea. 
Which makes me 😤AF

description:
A collection of various female Sanshin (god of mountain). ⁣
Each mural and painting is drawn differently and styles varies. ⁣
⁣
Female Sansin (산신) are called yeo-sansin (여산신) and can sometimes be called Sansin-halmae 신신할매 or Sansin Halmoni 산신할머니 referring to female mountain god as a doting and protective grandmother. ⁣
⁣
Note: Mudangs, the shamans refers to their gods in an affectionate manner by calling them 할머니 & 할아버지 (grandmother and grandfather) when addressing.⁣
⁣
⁣
Even the protective tiger deity thats always next to Sansin differs. Some painting would have a tiger, and others would have a leopard instead of the tiger. Both leopards and tigers were once native to Korea before going extinct. Traditionally its always been the tiger thats been the companion deity to Sansin. ⁣

description:
Mother's Day is bittersweet for me. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Mother's comes in all shapes, forms and sizes. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
I was 9 years old when my own mother walked out on us. My childhood memory of her - is her backside. Overnight I became "mom" to my  siblings who were 5 and 2 years old at the time. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
Fast forward 27 years⁣⁣
Reunited and reconnected with own my mom. She's is the most amazing grandmother to my children. As a mother, its all I can ever want for my boys to grow with the love from their grandmother. ⁣Sleeping in grandma's embrace and nourished by her meals. ⁣⁣

description:
Tonight, I am  missing my spirit mother, my dear elder. ⁣
⁣
It takes me less than 10 minutes to reach  her home. When I enter, I pay my respects to her gods first immediately bowing in the shrine.  Then I make my way greeting all the elders, asking if they all had a restful sleep with a cheerful good morning. ⁣
Sometimes spirit dad makes a smoothie - it looks like the 'grey stuff' from Disney Beauty & Beatst and its a warm!!!! 😑 Made with boiled onions, and all sorts of healthy god-knows-what. Haha. I usually hold my breath and gulp it down, smile respectfully, while I sternly turn down a second portion. ⁣
We always gather for a late breakfast, and I wait till every elder took a bite of their food, before I take mine. (Its how I was raised, but how I want to express my respect). I'm not a person for emotional words, instead I show through my actions big or small. ⁣
⁣
We spend all day together. Spirit dad would tell me the same stories again, and often we chatter up a storm. I've been told curiosity kills the cat. Whenever I see spirit mom, I overload her with many pondering questions that I try to be mindful not to abuse. I always start with...mom, can I ask a question ? Which she replies always. ⁣
⁣
Its been 5 or so weeks since I seen my spirit mother and I miss her. I call everyday to make sure everyone is okay. I nag to them, making sure they stay home, and volunteer to help with groceries and errands. ⁣
⁣
⁣
I was told by someone yesterday I need to share more. ⁣
⁣
⁣

Its time I say this, hopefully to clarify any misinformation. 

I am NOT a tarot card reader or work with any cards - I cannot give you the card of the day, or pull out a card for a quick yes/no. 
I am definitely not a hotline 1800 psychic. I dont give out free readings to advertise my services. This is not to disrespect to any practioners that work in those ways. I know so many respectable practioners who do but it is not my way of working. 

I work in the ways of my Korean ancestry. My divination sessions are different, using tools like coin tossing, rice throwing and flag pulling. Working with these items are directly related to the deities of our folk and indigenous beliefs. Our tradition even casting bones, rocks and sticks to read the energies and divinate.

Once I had a "psychic" come over to hang out, when I mistaken it for a session. She asked for advice and watched me pull flags and work in my ways. She asked why I use my tools as a crutch, when she can just use her clairvoyance without tool's. 
Let me attempt to clarify this.  Working with gods means to work in a mutual partnership, requires a relationship and conversations with the spirits - using those tools is a way to communicate and verify. 

Maybe @tweedandspandex and I should have another IG Live to discuss this.

description:
My maternal grandparents were farmers and business merchants. They knew how to work and cultivate the land -farmers, which meant they worked closely with spirits,  gods and the deities. 
Immigrating to the US in the late 80s, early 90s. Working with other Korean elders, they turned a local dump into a bustling farm co-op in NYC. ⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣
If you are on a picnic, or happen to eat your meal outside. Before you eat, take a little piece of our food and throw in the air 3 times while saying GOSURE or GOSURI.⁣⁣⁣
⁣⁣⁣
Grandma said this was just a simple and humble way of paying respect to spirits. The spirits, they eat first. ⁣⁣I remember her teachings, and when I have a picnic or a meal. I throw pieces of food yelling GOSURE GOSURE GOSURE 고수레. ⁣⁣⁣its seen as a respectful gesture of feeding the land, or wandering spirits. ⁣⁣⁣⁣
Thanking my grandmother for teaching me her wisdom. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣
This sacred rite, this respectful ⁣gesture and act is very present and active in the shaman cultures of Mongolia, and others. ⁣
⁣
⁣

The 신당 shrine of my spirit mother began to fill up with black baby chicks. I woke up unsure of the meaning and message of this dream - one thing I know is they were not good signs -bad omens. 
I ran over to spirit mother to share the details of my dream. I was anxious, scared and nervous. 
Spirit mom was concerned, said 'this child will later stray the wrong path' and the black chicks are those people who will follow her unknowingly. I spent the rest of the day in deep conversation with my elder about options, choices, fate and destinies. 

Initiation day finally arrived, a long 3 day ceremony thats utterly bittersweet. On the second day, the initiate began to have doubts, started to cry telling us she regretted this. She wanted us to stop, pack up her bags to leave and go home. She asked me to take her to the airport, so she can return home. My elder and other spirit sister's were in shock, we talked gently with her and the initiate decided to try again.

9 years ago this June, I was fired from the Sapphire NYC strip club, working as a supervisor/manager. During that time I was  a heavy cocaine user - spending more or less $400 a night, almost overdosing twice. 

I walked out of a 6 year abusive relationship, packed my bag with no where to go. I ended up homeless and eventually lived off a friend's couch. It was truly a difficult time with no one to rely on. 

Despite the hardships, and lack of stability I was incredibly clear minded. This very moment of my life is when I had my spiritual awakening. 

With bags packed, and no where to go. I ended up at the playground, and went on the empty swings. The sun was warm, and the breeze gently caressed my face - as I looked up to the sky.

At the exact moment, thinking of spirits and ancestors. The swing right next to me started to swing back and forth, along with me. It felt so warm and comforting like falling into a soft blanket. 

My guardians, ancestors and spirits have always been with me - even at my darkest days and moments. Blood of warriors and healers within me.  They've always been there to uplift me into becoming who I am today. 

And I am totally fucking unapologetic about it. 

I want to take the time and thank my amazing friend ❤ @hichaweon for always supporting me, encouraging me to be more visible and sharing my many, many stories.

Altar Offerings - FRUITS symbolizes abundance, wealth and fertility.

I often get questions about what types of offerings are allowed in the Korean folk traditions. In older times, offerings mattered depending on the region and what was available locally and choices limited. 

Nowadays with modern technology and logistics, we have access to fruit and food from all over the world than before. 

I was taught that peaches and other stone fruits are avoided. This has to do with peach tree being used for exorcism in chasing away negativity and warding off evil. Stone fruits only have one seed/pit and avoided but fruits with many seeds are used to symbolize abundance. 

Sometimes this is even confusing for me, peaches are avoided for another reason because of the fur fuzz on the skin but yet kiwis 🥝 are okay to use. 
Roses or any plants with thorns are avoided because it deter and prick the spirits but yet pineapples 🍍 are used. 
Fruits with only one pit/seeds are avoided but yet avocados 🥑are acceptable.

Its been 4.5 years since walking this path and I've been able to meet & connect with so many. 

I received an email, asking why my prices was expensive. They explained that they've worked with other mudangs and spirit workers. Then further inquired where my money is being spent. The asker was genuinely asking without trying to be rude and was really nice and kind. I answered the email in the best way I can - explaining what I do, and where I spend my money on. I was incredibly appreciative of the open and kind communication we had compared to the way others approached this with me. This is not to attack or shame the person who emailed but to show how a conversation can take place about this openly. 

Other people asked for healing ceremony and argued that healing should be free, or spirit work is free. You can't pour from an empty cup. When I have to explain my right to make an earning and support my family was incredibly upsetting.

A spirit sister complained (threw a tantrum) that I had a wider reach and following on social media as if that equates to money or something. She worked a normal job, living a single life while I depended on my spiritual work supporting my family with no other means.

My sessions are listed as 1 hour, but its 2 hours - the longest was 6hrs. Other mudang or spirit  workers may have jobs or other work to support themselves - but I dont. 

I dedicate my time/life to train in the traditional healing arts without any means of other financial income. I dont get any tax incentives or special writeoffs. I pay for everything like everyone else. 
It's interesting being in this position, called and accused of many things from others  like clout-chasing 🤣 when I am just sharing my path and stories. 

I've been supported by amazing female creators - that reminded me that I need to keep moving and opening myself to opportunities  instead of putting myself in a corner to continue doing my work as a mudang. I'm so damn grateful for their support and guidance, because in my hard times they kept cheering me on. Just as my gods and spirits have always held me up and provided.

description:
How did politics affect the Mudang and Korean Shamanism? ⁣
⁣
The ancient kings of Korea were often called different titles that referred to them as a shaman. Kings of Korea were seen as head shamans, leading rituals to worship the sun, the mountain, calling in the rain and performing exorcism rituals to appease malicious spirits.⁣
⁣
Buddhism and Confucianism was imported in the 4th Century.  While surrounding ancient nations adopted Buddhism but Silla held onto her shamanistic roots for another century before succumbing. ⁣
⁣
During the Joseon period (heavily Confucius) mudang were prohibited from entering the city (Hanyang, now Seoul). Mudangs were classified as dirty and the lowest social class. Hefty taxes and heavy fines was slapped on a mudang to deter their practices. ⁣
Its during this time, shamanism became the religion of the woman. ⁣
Its during a kut 굿 ceremony that women were allowed freely to express themselves in a repressed Confucian society.  Drinking, singing, dancing and releasing all the stress of a repressed life.⁣
During the Japanese Occupation, Mugyo or Musok was seen as dirty and lowclass. The Japanese attempted to replace Korean Shamanism with their Shinto. ⁣
⁣
A brutal blow to Korean shamanic roots was during "New Village Movement" (Saemaeul-ho Undong). Initiated in the 70s by President Park to eradicate anything that resembled shamanism. Most shrines and temples in rural countryside and elsewhere were torn down. A modern 'enlightened' movement to bring Korea to westernized. ⁣
⁣
⁣
And we survived. ⁣
Grew back stronger⁣
because our roots are too deep to ignore. ⁣
We come from a land of survival. ⁣
Our ancestors were badass survivors, who birthed and gave life to us. ⁣
We are a product of an amazing and resilient ancestral lineage. ⁣
💜✊⁣

애바위 which refers to the rock, the boulder where the young betrothed female was last seen. Her shrine is called 해신당 Haesindang, which has turned into a park with penis sculptures. ⁣

One version of her story says that she was standing on a rock, while her fiancee was fishing. A storm came sweeping her away.⁣

Kitchen spirit, 조왕신 Jowang-shin. Mythology says that Jowangshin (kitchen goddess) is the wife of the roof beam god 성주 Seongju.

Putting sticky taffy is believed to block the mouth of the kitchen spirit so they won't be able to tattle on you.

description:
I remember looking up to a vivid blue sky, with clouds dotted across. ⁣
A majestic white horse with wings flew and weaved in between the clouds.⁣
⁣
Then I woke up, and stayed up all night wondering about the dreams meaning. I was anxious to phone my spirit mum to tell her about it. ⁣
In Korean mythology, the Chollima is a mythical white horse with majestic wings at its sides, like a Korean pegasus. Only difference with the Korean Chollima is that this horse had smaller wings on each hoof like the Roman Mercury god with his winged feet. ⁣
The Chollima, is a mythical horse capable of lightning speed. It desired to become tamed, but no man was able to and instead flew up into the sky, never seen again. ⁣
⁣
The white horse is symbolic and very important to the surrounding areas of North Asia like Mongolia, Tuvan, Tibetan, N.Korea etc. ⁣
⁣
⁣
Spirit mom was happy and pleased to hear about my dream. She shared her wisdom and teachings, which is a very personal message for me. ⁣
⁣
⁣picture take at Ohdae Mountain in Korea. ⁣
⁣

In honor of Asian Pacific Islander Hertiage Month and Children's Day 어린이날. ⁣
⁣
Children's Day (May 5) is a holiday in Korea honoring children, started by an activist in 1923 during the time of the Japanese occupation.  As oppression grew, later 어린이날 was banned by the Japanese in 1939. ⁣
⁣
After the Korea War, celebration of 어린이날 resumed. ⁣
⁣
Mother's Day also started sometime in the 1930s and later changed to Parents Day to show equality towards fathers. ⁣
⁣
⁣
• • • • •⁣
⁣
⁣
I dont have much pictures of myself as a baby or growing child. When my parents divorced, my father in his raging kimchi temper threw out our albums.⁣ ⁣
Growing up, I was constantly subjected to head shaving. One head shaving occasion, I was gifted a wig. Apparently I hated the itchy and scratchy wig, that I threw it down  completely embarrassing my mother. ⁣
⁣
In preschool, my head was shaved again but this time I was given an entire new wardrobe. My mother dressed me up as a boy, and I loved it. ⁣I remember dressing up in boys clothing and feeling like I was given a superhero cape. As if it was permission to run wild, cause mishcief and play like the "boys". ⁣
⁣
⁣Looking back...my mother often says alot of my childhood events foreshadowed the telling of my becoming into a mudang. ⁣
⁣
⁣
Head shaving was very common to do, still practiced by some. An old wives tale, to promote hair thickness and growth. ⁣

description:
Ritual ceremony prop called 고 - go. The 'go' comes in various colors, and for each kut ceremony we prepare about 4. ⁣
Different color go are knotted and prepare for use, when the ancestral spirits are summoned. Each ancestor that enters the ritual space and the mudang, grabs a colored go and begins to shake out the knots of the go with ritual music. ⁣
⁣
The go is a very important ritual prop with rich symbolism.  The color of the go is symbolic, an indicator of ancestral han. The spirits that are consumed by their han, uses the black colored go. Its the spirits, that uses the black go...we have to send off properly and respectfully with compassion.  The knots tied on the go, represents the different realms of the underworld. ⁣
Traditionally money is folded into each knot of the go, used as offerings for each guardian of the underworld. ⁣
⁣
During the kut, of the ancestors gori the spirit sometimes tear the go in half, and walks through it as the fabric is ripped along the way. This is very symbolic, because it shows the ancestors is breaking through their own han, and shows the ancestors travelling through the underworld as we guide them to the gates of the spirit realm. ⁣
⁣

description:
달래 Dahle ⁣
⁣
Korean wild chives or known as mountain chives called dahle.  Same family as garlic, onions and shallots. ⁣
Its symbolic for the incoming spring, and part of the 5 spicy vegetables called oshinchae - and considered a vegetable with  5 virtues.⁣
Its one of the spring vegetables that was offered to the king as tribute. Even a korean folk song sung since the Joseon dynasty tells the story of children running around eating peppers and dahle while dad went out. ⁣
⁣
Dahle was used as folk medicine- as a means to stimulate a person's appetite.  Dahle had uncanny ability to break through the frozen soil, and was eaten to give our ancestors vitality and strength. ⁣
⁣
Mom foraged these right in our yard, growing naturally and abundantly. ⁣
⁣

description:
The Sanshin shrine in the Korean Buddhist temple of Jeondeungsa. ⁣
⁣
Koreas mountain worship is found throughout the peninsula. Our shamanic god of the mountain, Sanshin 산신, the mountains is symbolic for the axis of the world. ⁣
Sanshin god of mountain is always depicted with a tiger, and some rarer paintings it would depict 3 tigers. The oldest Sanshin painting is housed in Mount Inwang and roughly dated back to the 1700s. ⁣
산신 are traditionally drawn in a seated position, with a white fan made from the feathers of a white crane. White crane in korean culture is symbolic for high status, longevity, wisdom, etc. Sanshin is always dressed in color red, although some modern paintings have 산신 in other forms and colors. Along with the tiger, 산신 also have children attendees Dong-ja & Dong-yeo. ⁣
⁣
While most mountains and Sanshin are depicted as an elderly man, some mountains in Korea are said to be inhabited by a female Sanshin, a Yeo-Sanshin. The most famous 여산신 (yeo-sanshin) of Korea is 지리산 (Mt. Jiri) and 계룡산 (Mt. Gyerong). Some temples will have 탱화 taeng-hwa (mural) of both male Sanshin god with the female yeo-sanshin. ⁣
⁣
⁣

description:
Part 2/2⁣
⁣
All the various and different paths of the many 무당 (shaman) is like the unique houses or buildings lined up on a city block. Each house is different, having custom styles and designs. No two house is the same, but then strip away the cosmetics and exteriors. ⁣
Look at their bones and structures they are the same. All built with a sturdy foundation, with supporting walls and a protective roof. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣This is how I view the many paths of 무당's today. My advice is do not replace the sacred, instead add-on to it enriching your practice. For the modern 무당, I say learn the way its been practiced, then bring in your modern elements once you understood the valuable teachings of the tradition. ⁣⁣
(Example, learn to perform divination in traditional way as it helps makes you exercise your ability to establish connection with the gods. Learn to understand the language and tone of the spirits through use of traditional tools. Afterwards teach and work with the spirits to learn the language of modern ways and tools) ⁣
⁣.
.
Obviously this isnt a 'one size fits all'... but it can help find your methods. Some times the gods have something else different planned out than what you want. ⁣
I thought I was going to blend traditional Korean shamanism with modern spiritual practices. Truthfully, traditions scared me. I did not want to fully accept the 'daunting' burden', and wanted to bring in modern elements that made it easier to practice, making it more convenient path to accept and walk. ⁣
⁣
⁣Obviously, my gods had a different plan than I did

description:
Today is World Refugee Day. ⁣⁣
I am a child of immigrants parents, and my parents are children of refugees. When the Korean war erupted, my maternal grandmother left her entire family behind. She embarked on a solo journey on foot climbing over mountains walking towards the South. She never realized that our ancestral land would be divided. She pass away without ever seeing or hearing from her family. ⁣⁣
Stories like my grandmother is common among our grandparents generation. Our parents suffered as post war babies, with little to no food and clothes. ⁣⁣
Today in America, the Trump administration has locked up infants, young children and teens in groups without proper food and water. I read the news today about a young 2 year old toddler, sick with the flu, diaperless and being looked after the older children. ⁣My heart broke for that child and others. ⁣
I remember many times in my life when I wished someone spoke out for me, stood up for me and protected me. It was until I got older that I had to stand up for myself, voicing myself. Now that I am the adult, I hope to be....what I didnt have when I was young. ⁣⁣
⁣In a world, where thousands of families with children are fleeing for their lives, if you can please help donate any funds to help the migrant children. If you cant donate money, find the nearest local refugee resettlement agency and donate goods there. ⁣⁣
⁣
⁣
Picture taken at 강천사, 전라북도⁣
Gangcheonsa,  Jeolla-bukdo⁣

description:
The offering table and spread for the ancestors. ⁣
I took the picture from this perspective to show, why we set the offerings in this way.  When we are facing the table, we are facing the ancestors. From our view, the first offerings is fruit but turn it around. Then from the ancestors POV, it's the last row. ⁣
The structure of setting an offering table is very practical. The first row of offerings would be their rice, with water and soup. Next row, is their side dishes (banchan) to enjoy with their rice. Then comes the liquor, with rice cakes, cookies, candy, sweets and fruit - the dessert round 'so to speak'. ⁣
Customarily, we would put money on the rice cakes to ask for blessings and luck. Money was also put on the candy plate for the children spirits of the family. ⁣
⁣
When we speak about ancestors, we refer to blood ancestry and those who we have fated destinies (인연) with, like in adoption and step parents. ⁣⁣Of course, having more family means more work for us. 😅⁣ 🙏
⁣

description:

Homemade 막걸리 makgeolli 🍶 ⁣
⁣
The light sparkling rice wine is the oldest agrarian spirit beverage in Korea. The tradition of makgeolli goes back to the ancient Three Kingdom Era and predates soju. Known as the peasant wine, the 'farmers  liquor' it was the drink of the farmers, the working class. ⁣
Makgeolli is also a traditional offering that is used in every ceremony and rituals. It's used in giving offering to the land, the house gods, wandering homeless spirits and many other ritual, rites and ceremonies. ⁣
⁣
Modern Ritual for Car⁣ 🚙
If your car has been in the shop for repairs or maintenance. We give pour a little bit of makgeolli or any liquor on each wheel - to give as offering and blessing. ⁣
Just like when our homes undergo any renovation and construction, the spirit of the home and land is disturbed. While a 고사 gosa ritual is performed for a home or a business spirits., we pour liquor on the car wheels. ⁣

description:
Dad, brought a box of Korean grapes for the kids and family. But before we can open, wash and devour it... it must be offered up in my shrine. ⁣
While the gesture may not seem like much, but it's a huge act of respect. The spirits eat before me, they are taken care of before me. A mudang should ONLY look to her gods, and those shaman with strong gods, their gods would expect that much. It's the reason why mudangs left their families, their parents and children, starting anew. Why? ⁣
A shaman is a vessel, a living embodiment of the gods but not every shaman is the same as their abilities varies. ⁣
Think of it like this...mudangs are conductor of the spirit world, just like copper's great conductors for electricity. Not all conductors are the same despite their qualifications.  I don't know what type of conductor I will be. ⁣
⁣
When making water offerings, those with traditional bowls will come with a lid. Offering bowls must never have a lid on or closed.  The lid should be placed to the left of the bowl, and all altar items should be washed weekly, which is a ritual itself. Same thing for your incense, its should be placed to the right of your incense pot. These are the little details that are often overlooked but necessary in creating proper foundations of our work. Everything is intentional and mindful, awareness must be present at all times. Not something that is easy for myself either, as I am still learning despite the few years already.⁣
I may have the marks of the gods, the necessary ingredients to make me a Mudang. But that doesnt mean, or guarantee me success as one. It's all about how deep our relationship with our gods are. ⁣
⁣

description:
Often asked, why I dont have statues or idols of the gods in my shrine. A shrine can be either called 'shindang' or 'beobdang', a shindang means the hall of the gods, and beobdang means the law, hall of rules -with Buddhist influence.⁣⁣
⁣⁣
For practical reasons is why I dont have statues or idols of my gods - also, I just dont connect with the idol figures. The idol statues are more of a recent representation of the spirits...natural objects , paintings or calligraphy were used. Instead of the statues, I use their tools and items as their symbolic representation. Each tool and item treated and handled with respect as the spirits energy is alive. ⁣⁣
⁣
Every shrine will be different according to each mudang, their lineage, their personal style and their spirits taste. Every shindang (shrine) varies. Personally for myself and my gods, we dont like clutter and perfer to have a more simpler set up. While other mudangs will have stacks of offerings and paraphernalia which suits their style. ⁣⁣
⁣⁣

Today is Parents Day. 
In Korea, May 8th was originally celebrated as Mothers Day, but then came the question about the fathers. And so was born Parents Day!! 🥳
Its purpose was to teach the youth about paying respect to their elders, since Korea was a confucian society. 
A Tuvan shaman friend told me that this day is also celebrated in Russia. Families prepare food offerings for their ancestors as well. 
This picture was taken at Gangwondo, Korea. That day, my spirit mom took me to DMZ, since my family were from that region. 
Woke up at 4am and witness another beautiful sunrise. .

description:
What's the etiquette of visiting a mudangs shrine/temple?⁣ Alot of people ask me, what is the proper way and behavior of the sindang [신당] shrine/temple. Many arent accustomed to the traditions. At one point, I too, didnt know what the proper etiquettes were but I will share what I know. ⁣
☆Entering the shrine room, you may light an incense if you desire to. Proper respects is to bow, in a sets of 3 or 9 full body bows. If bowing is difficult, then bow your head with your hands together in the prayer form.⁣
☆Never have your back turned towards the altar, the gods are facing towards you, so be mindful not to show your back. ⁣
☆Sitting on the floor in the shrine room [traditional style] on floor cushions, for some it may be difficult. You can stretch your legs out but dont point your feet towards the altar. ⁣
☆No cursing, be mindful of the language used.⁣
☆Set your offerings on the altar whether its payment for a reading or other types of offerings. ⁣
What can you bring as an offering?⁣
Fruit (no stone fruit), liquor (*no makkoli rice wine), cakes, rice cakes, cookie, candy, pastry goods, rice or money. Offerings must be new, purchased with the intentions to use as offerings. Not something laying around in your pantry/fridge. ⁣
• Makkoli rice wine [막걸리] is an offering usually given to the low end spirits so cant be used as an offering to the gods. ⁣
⁣

alt_text: Photo by Mudang Jenn 무당젠 on December 23, 2019.

description:
Few years back, the drums came for me. 
I was always anxious, I couldnt sleep, I couldnt eat, I wasnt comfortable at all.

At night, visions would terrify me leaving me petrified. I would see the shadows move about in the room. 
In the shower as I wiped the water off my face, my eyes went blank, my vision blurred,  grayed and blacked out. I couldnt see for a few seconds but it felt like forever. I freaked out, screamed, and yelled for my husband. He went with me everywhere,  to the bathroom when I need to pee and shower. He was always there to be my human shield, my knight. 
I could hear the drums banging, and it would only start at night. When I closed my eyes, the drums sounded louder, making me miserable. The sounds of the  drums was accompanied by the intense desire to run into the woods, the forest. Over time, I felt trapped and had thoughts of abandoning my family to run into the mountains. 
I grew severely depressed, and sleep deprived due to the endless 가위눌려, 'sleep paralysis '. Not to mention the chronic pain, the multiple surgeries I've gone through. 
I went to many healers, psychics, witches, mediums, and shamans. I was told that I had a curse done on my family, from my mother's side. Not one was able to help me, and I'm convinced some of them made it worse for me...messing with something they shouldnt of. 
Now, I look at all my horrific past experiences and I understand now.  There's a saying in Korean "그릇을 만들어"...means to make a bowl/dish. It refers to the process of shaping, pounding and working with clay to make the dish/bowl you need. ⁣
⁣
⁣
My gods shaped and molded to be the "bowl" they needed me to be. 🍵

description:
There was a branch of korean shamanism that specifically worshipped Dangun as a god only. Gosindo (way of the ancestral God) , was the ancient form of Dangun worship. 
That sect of Korean shamanism was wiped out and died by the 15th century. The legend of Dangun played a vital role during the Mongolian invasion of Korea, where it helped with national unity and mobilization against. 
Due to the resurgence of Korean nationalism from the invasion and occupation of Japan.  Gosindo 고신도 was reborn as Daejongism during the Japanese occupation, and helped the Korean independence movement. Many controversy due the cult-like sects that arose. 
The roots of Dahn Yoga claims that they have the same practices as Dangun did when he first ruled over Korea . 
Picture taken from Google,  a ceremony/ritual for Dangun with his altar of offerings.

description:
When we have a 고사 (gosa) for a place of business, then each entrance/exit will have an offering of red bean rice cake, and a cup of makkoli (rice wine). If there is a kitchen within the business,  another offering is set for the kitchen godess Jowangshin 조왕신. ⁣
⁣
If it's a place with many machinery and power tools, like of a contractor or a warehouse,  we set the offerings of rice cake and makkoli at each location. ⁣
The red bean in our korean shamanic culture are used to perform exorcism, cleansing and chasing of any negative energy and luck. The red bean rice cake serves as a food offering that wards off negativity and lowly bad spirits. ⁣
To bring in luck, prosperity and fruitful blessings a pig offering, is necessary. Depending on the price paid by the client, if the client wanted a super grand gosa, then we would of used a whole pig, or even a whole cow. On top of that meat offerings, we put money dipped in makkoli all over the offerings. ⁣
When leaving money to the mudang, during a gosa. Its proper respect and customary to put an envelope on top of the red bean rice cake (as shown)⁣
⁣

description:
Moon Rabbit ⁣
With the mid-autumn festival , it reminded me of the Legend of the Moon Rabbit or Jade Rabbit. The moon during the Chiseok is believed to be the brightest and fullest, symbolizing abundance and prosperty. The Moon Rabbit (Jade Rabbit) lives on the moon, pounding a huge mortar with rice to make rice cakes. ⁣
⁣
Legend goes the Emperor of Heaven decided to test the faith and loyalty of the rabbit, fox and monkey. Emperor disguised as a beggar asked the fox, monkey and rabbit to bring food to eat. ⁣
Monkey returned with fruit, fox returned with fish but the rabbit was only able to bring grass. Feeling ashamed, the rabbit lit the grass on fire, jumped into it sacraficing itself. Touched by such sacrafice, the emperor placed the Rabbit on the moon to become the guardian. ⁣
Modern day story includes two rabbit, people thought the one rabbit was too lonely and sent a friend. Two rabbits making rice cakes under a cinnamon tree symbolizes the coming together of family. ⁣

description:
Happy Lunar New Year 🎉⁣
We call this celebration, Seollal 설날. Its a family holiday celebrating the 1st day of the Lunar Metal Rat Year. ⁣
⁣
Spent all day cooking, and luckily my partner was home to help assist me. Fruit, liquor, water, vegetables, fritters, rice cakes, meat, fish, desserts and traditional snacks was all laid out. ⁣
⁣
Most important offering of 떡국 ttuk-guk (rice cake soup) a traditional dish eaten on Seollal. The eating a bowl of ttuk-guk symbolizes good health and growing a year older. Its thought that this customary practice originated in ancient times. During the Goryeo period it was one of the major holidays to pay worship to ones ancestors. ⁣
⁣
Its also customary for communities to visit their local mudang (shaman) to participate in exorcism and cleansing ritual prayers. For some families, an important part of their customs as it drives away any negative influences protecting them for the new year. ⁣
⁣

description:
Todays 굿 Kut ceremony offerings have been all set in the morning before we gather for breakfast. ⁣
⁣
Especially on a day with a ritual, ceremony or special holiday the spirits - either the gods 신 (shin) or the ancestors 조상 (josang) eats first. ⁣
⁣
In the Korean customs, when gathering at the dinner table or any table to eat....no one lifts their spoon or take a sip of water until the family elder takes their first bite. In my home, we all gathered at the table every meal but did not eat until Grandpa (the elder) or my dad picked his spoon up and took a bite. ⁣
⁣
This is also why, whenever I go grocery shopping I put all the fruits on my altar to offer my gods, ancestors and spirits - the first bite of our food. Eating food thats been blessed by our ancestors is another ritual we call eumbok. Means we receive the blessings of the gods and spirits through the food we offered. ⁣
⁣⁣
Thank you to everyone whose been so understanding,  I had to cancel and reschedule alot of my appointments because of the kut ceremony I was called into. ⁣
⁣
Wishing everyone a wonderful New Year. ⁣ ⁣

description:
Woke up around 4am.⁣
Its prime time for prayers, its supposedly when spirit connection is at its peak. When we go to Korea for pilgrimage, we also pray in the mountains and at sacred shrines at this time. Whenever I am disturbed by spirits or energy, I stir  around this time. ⁣
⁣
When there is no 굿 kut ritual ceremonies scheduled, and I wake at this time. I take it as a sign, a gentle nudge by my gods to "have a chat"...called into prayers. Before I step into my 신당 (shindang; shrine of gods), I must be clean so I hop in for a early morning bath. ⁣
When I enter my 신당, I give my morning greetings. Fresh water offerings are poured, candles are lighted and incense sticks are lit by the candleflames. The flame that lights the incense must never be blown out with our mouth, instead it's much more proper to 'shake' out the flame. It's a mindful and respectful gesture, just like vacuums cleaners are avoided in a temple, instead I use dry swiffer cloths to clean. Every act and behavior within the temple should be very mindful and intentional, it's an act of respect while in the presence of the gods. ⁣
⁣

description:
Happy Winter Solstice!⁣
Dongji 동지!⁣
⁣
Its a symbolic day, and the traditional ritual includes cooking patt-juk, red bean porridge.  A small bowl of red bean porridge is served to every room in the house - bedrooms, bathrooms,  closet, foyers, the kitchen, etc. In older times, people would spray the red bean porridge over their doors and windows. ⁣
⁣
The red color from the red bean possesses the ability to ward off evil and expell lowly spirits that may be within the home. Containing yang energy and effective to counter the yin-energy spirits.  Eating ppat-juk is very closely tied and connected to the agarian roots of the Korean culture and recognized as a sacrafical ritual food. ⁣
⁣
The folktale goes a man named Gong-Gong ssi, had a son who died on Dongji and later became the spirit of smallpox disease. He hated red beans and so it was cooked every Dongji to keep him away. ⁣
⁣

description:
Sam-saek Namul 삼색 나물.
⁣
The tri-colored vegetable, a direct result of the Buddhist influence since the Three Kindom Era along with the ban of meat. With the Mongol invasion and the ban was lifted, meat offerings were used for rituals like jesa (ancesreal rites) ⁣
⁣
The three vegetable represents root, stem and leaf, and the colors white, green and brown. All coming together to emody prosperity. ⁣
⁣
The white root of the bellflower respresents our ancestors, the root and foundation of any family. The brown stems of the fern braken represents the support of our parents (the present). Lastly, the green leafs represents the future of the family. ⁣
⁣
Many ask me, when they set their offering tables if it is mandatory to have all dishes? Can I just have rice and fritters, or just rice cakes?⁣
There are times when I just have fruit or just rice cakes. But then again, I do my full offering in my shrine monthly and small offerings -daily. ⁣
⁣
I can't tell you what you should do, because our traditions and customs clearly speaks for itself. Setting an offering spread requires you to spend money, and for those who have a hard time financially - its difficult. If you can only afford some fruits only, I am positive your spirit will be touched by the offerings, although small but speaks in volumes about your respect and dedication. ⁣
⁣
⁣
⁣

description:
How long does it take to train as a mudang [korean shaman]. Most mudangs takes about 3 years or so to learn the way of our spirits. Traditional, when one finds the appropriate lineage and teacher, the mudang-to-be would enter their elders home. Help in the day to day life of their elder, shadowing their every move. Even doing mundane tasks of helping her spirit mother clean their home, cook, and run daily errands. This is true especially for the low hierarchy apprentice, who needs to work their way up in the skills. 
Most Korean mudangs here in the US, dont have the basic training. Usually going to Korea to get their initiation,  unable to commit to shadowing their spirit mother, without any training or guidance. This I feel can be a very slippery slope, as most wouldnt know how to proceed with shrine care duties of their temple,  setting up of offerings, aiding clients with rituals and ceremonies. To me this is very worrisome,  as the newbie mudangs are left unguided. Its imperative that the newbie mudangs keeps in constant contact with their elder, to learn, grow and to discuss. 
It's like as if someone who graduated to be a doctor but never step foot in a hospital or a clinic, how would they know to provide patient care. 
One thing I find to struggle with, is when in prayer our spirits communicate. Sometimes we may think the spirits is telling us something,  when in fact it's hard to decipher if its really the case due to our desire and wants. 
In my case, since I am searching for a new apartment.  I ask my spirits if this place is good to be seated, they say yes because I really loved the newly renovated place. But bring my spirit mother over to take a look, she disproves because the energy of the land, the spirits of this home is too chaotic, which can interfere with my work. Dismiss a teacher lead to chaos. 
On our way Ilwolsan, I stopped to prayed briefly at the altar of the fairy maiden Sonyeo. 선녀
