description:
(Part 1/3)  4am prayers at Seon-bawi #선바위, the main sacred point of Mt. Inwangsan in Seoul.  It's noted that even Korea's past Kings came here to pray and meditate. 
Seon-bawi or Gijaam is one the world's most worshipped rock, the primary reason why it's considered one of the holiest mountain. Below the Seon-bawi or Gijaam lays the Guksa-dang #국사당 - the National Shaman Spirit shrine, therefore enhancing and enforcing the sacredness. 
This rock natural formation is call Gijaam because in the past married woman came here to pray for child-bearing. Or others say, the rock looks like a monk wearing robes, and is called meditation rock. Some say the rock resembles King Taejo founding King of Joseon along with his Queen or his close friend Master Monk Muhak. 
Others say, they see the rocks as the great monks sitting in contemplation and protection of Seoul city. And some maintain the 'original' ancient views with a mystical twist of male/female Buddha's to help relieve sufferings. 
Historically, when King Taejo founded Joseon his friend Master Monk Muhak wanted to include Seon-bawi within the city walls, but royal advisor and leading Neo-confucianist 'Sambong'  advocate to exclude them, symbolically excluding Korea's native indigenous shaman culture. 
At the mountain peak sits a natural rock figure which is said to be the Benevolent King himself or Sansin (Mountain god). Next to him is a rock figure of his tiger (guardian) and a dark magpie stone figure perched behind.

description:
People are usually divided in regards to anything spiritual. Are mediums/psychic/shamans real, fakes or frauds? 
The one question I absolutely f***king hate is, how come you dont know lottery numbers. Or asking me to "predict" some petty BS like its a circus freak show.

Or how about someone who is employed at the lottery, shouldn't they know what numbers are going to pick the lottery winner? 
I will never claim to be 100%, because there is no such damn thing.  Can a doctor cure every person that walks into their office, NOPE. 
I have had very few clients who I didn't connect with, to me...that just means that our destiny/fate path didn't cross. But when I do connect, which is the majority of my clients...its a beautiful thing.

my husband tells me, when he talks about a person..."I hope youre not trying to feel him/her". I get angry becuz I don't control it... Sometimes spirits just pop up & talks, you cant run anywhere because they follow you.

description:
I am constantly learning more about my shaman culture, and often includes the politics and history.

When Japan first took over Korea, it is said that the Japanese recognize the spirits (Heavenly) of and the Ki (energy). They determined that to break the strong spirits, Koreans must receive their energy from our mountain. (One of Koreas most important shamanic god is Sansin, god of mountain)
The Japanese hired Shamans and feng shui masters to map out vital points of where the energy or spirit of Sansin is alive. They strategically drove iron stakes into the mountain, purpose of it is to kill the spirits. 
After Japan lost, Korea set off a new program promoting hiking to it's people. Asking it's people to climb the mountain to search for those iron stakes and rods that were driven into the mountains.  So that's how Korea became a country that it's people love to hike. 
To this day, there are some hikers that still carry on the mission of restoring order and the spirits back to Korea.

description:
I've arrived in Gangwon-do 강원도 after praying at Seoraksan 설악산 and Odaesan 오대산. 
Tomorrow, I will be making offerings and praying to the Dragon King of the East sea. Afterwards I will be right by the DMZ (Koreas Demilitarized Zone) that separates North Korea from South Korea. Spirit mom is granting my request to stop by the zone so I can finally pay my respects. 
Although I can't enter, I will make prayers and small offerings table. My ancestors came from North Korea before the war. My maternal grandmother was the only one in her family who made her journey safely before settling down in 파주 Paju. Grandmother never spoke of her past, family or any trauma that she endured. Instead she kept on living and she kept on going, despite the hardships. She became a refugee of sorts during the war, and had to resettle. 
Paternal grandpa came from the North too, and as the war broke out grandpa was forced to join the military and fight for the Japanese side during WWII. He even spoke of another family he had, when he lived in Japan while serving the military.  He had a wife and child, and when the war was over. Again, he was forced out of Japan and separated from his family. He was never able to establish contact,  and passed away in 2012. 
I wanted to go, so I can pay respects to the gods and most importantly pay homage to my ancestors. I know they have been waiting for me. 📿

description:
Korea has long been a shamanic country, every person had multiple shrines and altar with a danji within their homes.  A danji is earthenware jar that enshrines a sacred deity that is worshipped. Just a few decades ago, people still had a separate shrine room to serve their ancestral spirits performing jaesa and other duties to their spirits. Koreans are very spirited people and nation. 
Even common folks knew how to perform basic shamanic rituals without the aid of a mudang. The village mudang will teach others  to perform simple cleansing and exorcism rituals to maintain peace and harmony within the household. Some even had fortune telling intuition but that still wasnt enough to be marked as a mudang. 
Nowadays there is a huge spiritual movement, I get many inquiries from alot of people. Being a mudang is not the only path in my shamanic culture. If one feels compelled to serve the spirits, its usually our ancestors. They are our anchors, and our axis that serves to connect our spirited realm of the gods and deities. Some are inevitably marked and chosen by the spirits, but there is 2 types of markings. 
It makes me happy to know many are seeking the path to become more spirited like our ancestors before. It was the way of life to respect nature, to pay our respects to the natural world.

description:
Mala beads. A very sacred tool for many different cultures, tied with buddhism.

description:
There different types of shaman...
And there are different types of mudang. 
My spiritual lineage is of the heavenly celestial gods, than having a lineage line rooted in the earth bound spirits. 
The difference between mudangs whose spiritual lineage is rooted by celestial gods vs earth gods is the energy type. Also the way we finish our initiation differs... Mudangs with celestial lineage will "ride a pot filled with clean water", that earthen pot signifies the dragon god and we (mudang) neeed to strive to become as clear and clean as the water which we ride. 
Other initiation requires the dancing on top of the butcher knives. While both is a sign that the mudang has received her title/authority from the spirits...they are different. 
Mudangs with lineage in the Earth bound gods tend to be more aggressive, confrontational, demeanor is sassy, smoking, drinking, cursing and behavior isnt so refined. While I need to be more conscious of my actions...polish my rock, carry the burdens of my family and spirits, need to be better, self sacrifice. Responsibility are the same, type of work we do are the same....but there is a small difference
The work we do is the same, we perform ceremonies and invoke our gods to help those who seek the help of gods whether its related to health/sickness, luck/fortune, ancestors relief, love/marriage, etc.

If a person failed to be a successful mudang, then eventually became a giaseng. The giaseng training of art and beauty is the same exact training a mudang did, at least back in traditional times. The traditional dance shows of salpuri or pansori all birthed from a mudang's pain, the spirit pain.

description:

Awakening or Enlightenment is such a destructive process, its a sacred destruction. For me, happened a few times mixed with the calling of the spirits. It was hell on Earth, not a casual conversation you can talk about with your bestie. 
Before accepting this path, the few people I would open up to about this probably looked at me like I was a crazy person. Rambling on and talking about the fear of being marked, chosen and seeing things unexplainable.

description:
The weather in Korea has been so mild, alot warner than expected. Despite the cold air of the mountains, we were really lucky with the mildness. Everyday the sun shined "햇빛 쨍쨍" but the day I left Korea the clouds rolled in, the gloominess of the sky and rain began to fall.

description:
MU•DANG
What does it mean? Why do I use this term to call myself as opposed to a MAN•SHIN. 
The word itself is a term with great respect. 
MU means spirits, the shaman. DANG means an altar [in simple terms]. Some say this part refers to Dangun the founder of Korea, the grandson of the Heavenly King and of the motherly Bear. 
MUDANG means a living altar for the spirits,  for the gods [신] it is the epitome of what it means to be a shaman. A sacrificial lamb of sorts, I am the sacrifice,  the living altar for my spirits. A life path dedicated to my spirits,  whom I serve with every step, every breath. 
I dont choose to call myself a Manshin meaning [ten thousand spirits], I reserve that term for my elders, the veteran mudangs. How does one become a manshin? In my humble opinion,  a mudang becomes a manshin by having multiple initiations. Its during this initiations [맞이굿] that that different gods enter and leave the pantheon of the mudang. In time, the spirits the mudang encounters will be ten thousand, therefore being called a Manshin. 
Most Korean shamans, dont call themselves mudang because of the negativity that surrounds it. But I embrace it, despite what others may do because the title reminds me of the burden I must carry, the weight of my ancestors. My path isnt laid out with the red carpet, the insights and the deep lessons I learned is from falling many times. From learning under the wing and the guidance of my amazing spirit mother.
🙏

description:
"Once you carry your own water, you value each drop" - Author Unknown .
.
This echoes the same sentiments I try to express when I try to explain the very simple act of water offerings. 
A teacher took on a young apprentice, and one of the first tasks to learn, was to fetch the teacher a bowl of water everyday. Each day when the apprentice gave her a bowl of water, the teacher spilled it out. Every morning after morning,  the same thing happened. The apprentice tried to figure out what she did wrong, so she ask if the teacher wanted warm water, or cold water, room temperature, or flavored water. Each time she asked a question, the teacher just replied to bring a bowl of water. Months went by, and finally the apprentice had a tantrum fit, crying about. 
The teacher sternly told her, if you cant complete a simple task as fetching a bowl of water, then you dont deserve to learn under me. The basics of your foundation must be strong, and yet you fail at bringing a bowl of water. 
The apprentice picked up the bowl, and every morning she continued and each time the teacher spilled it out. Then one day, the apprentice took her time and pondered about the water. This time, she thoughtfully boiled the water with ginger, cooled it down and brought it to her teacher. This time it wasnt spilled out, and instead the teacher asked to explain.
The apprentice said, she realized the task wasnt about the water at all. It was never ever about the water.  It was about the heart and the emotion she carried while performing the task of fetching the water.
.
It's this deep meaningful message I hope to teach to my spirit sisters and my clients. One of the first things we do, is pour water offerings. Of course we pour fresh new water, but it isnt about the water. Instead it's about our hearts and mind while performing these tasks. The ability to look deeper in, the understanding of respect and mindfulness. description:
Today is the full moon,  and we are in the sindang [temple/shrine room] of my beloved spirit mother. We are gathered here to perform a special kut ceremony/ritual, a 49th day ritual. 
The clients father in law recently departed from this world, and to help him transition peacefully and harmonious,  we held a kut in his honor and of his ancestral spirits. 
For a ritual like this, we set up a special table with rice formed into a shape of a person. We take offerings that will be given to the spirit and lay it over the table with special ritual coverings making sure the figure isnt disturbed. 
We call the spirits of the clients, their ancestors one by one including her father in law. We gift them food, liquor and clothing to wear from the offering table. Each ancestor comes and spend their time speaking of their stories of grief or happiness, as they release their traumas through storytelling. 
After all the spirits are sent away, and the ritual has come to a close. We remove the rice figure coverings and a new shape or imprint will form. Giving us insight to the new form the ancestor spirit has taken like a bird, dog, wolf, bear, etc. This is the new form the spirit has taken in on their travel back to the heavenly world of our ancestors. 
I hope that when I return back to my spirits and ancestors,  I can do so with integrity, dignity and honor. I hope they I did my ancestors proud with my work here.

description:

제사 [Jesa] the offerings table spread for ancestors. 
Alot of people ask why the fruits are the 1st row of offerings. Actually,  it's not. Between the candles, is the ancestors tablet with their names written down, that's where the ancestors spirits "sit", and when facing the offering table from their perspective...the fruits are the last course, like for dessert and to aid in digestion after a meal. 
Did you know that traditionally, when a family member passes away. An offering table is set in their room, everyday for 3 years. That's 1,095 days total of offering tables set up, meals prepared. 
The offering table very basic requirements is rice, water, liquor with 3 vegetable sides [of different colors], jeon [veggie/meat fritters], maybe some rice cakes and fruit offerings. 
Candles and incense are always needed at any offering tables. The candles "light up" the offerings showing it to the spirits so it can be seen, the incense guide the spirits to the offerings, the incense call the spirits in. 
Those who want to set up offerings but cannot, usually commission a mudang to set up their table with the basic offerings. Its usually households with a Christian background that still calls me, requesting the jesa offering table.

description:
Many Korean diasporas reach out to me about reconnecting back to their ancestral roots. Most are interested in learning about the ancestral traditions of our culture, our indigenous shamanic practice & beliefs that dates back to prehistory.
Roots. Our roots are important. 
A flower plant cannot survive without their roots, it's through the roots they are able to grow. If the roots of that plant become diseased, then slowly the plant itself becomes diseased as well. 
Ancestral veneration (worship) is important and to honor them would be a kut 굿 ceremony. Through this ancestral kut ceremony, can we treat those with diseased roots. And since those roots are hidden away underneath the dirt, unseen to the plant. In the ceremony, we open the doors of the spirits, inviting them in to tell us their story, their joys/pains. alt_text: Photo by Mudang Jenn 무당젠 on August 25, 2016.

description:
The ancient altar of Dangun known as 'Chamseongdan' located at Manisan 마니산. Manisan has been a site for shamanic worship since ancient times. Some shamans consider this a 'demon expelling' mountain and this very mountain to have the strongest 'Ki' energy of Korea. 
This altar is said to have been built by Dangun himself. Dangun the founder of Korea (2333 BC) offered sacrifices and ritual ceremonies to the heavens here. This site is believed to be over 4000 years old, underwent a few renovations but still maintain its original form and shape. The tradition of offering sacrifices continued on with the 3 Ancient Kingdoms of Silla, Baekji and Goguryeo kings even up to the Joseon period. 
Ceremonies are still held here yearly.
This site also houses the Korean hornbeam tree regarded as the oldest and most beautiful of its species, designated as a cultural asset in '09.
Based on the legend, Dangun ruled as king for over 1500 years. At the age of 1908 years old,  he retreated into the mountains and became immortal Sanshin the god of mountain.  It is said this mountain represents heaven,  and I couldn't agree more. 
I sat here  in silent prayers despite the screaming winds, thought I might literally be blown away. This mountain feels as if I am standing at the entrance of heaven with the gods.

Someone asked if a shaman is the same as a fortune teller and vice versa.

Because of the spirits,  and the negative influence/affect of the recently passed spirit which we call Samu ssal. 
A properly initiated mudang, or even an experienced veteran mudang cannot withstand the winds of Samu-ssal. The bad luck and energy of a persons passing can affect us, negatively. Performing an exorcism can help, but still wont be able to fully neutralize the negativity of Samu ssal. 
Traditionally,  when a person passes away they are given 49 days to 'wander around' and tie up loose ends, seeking their closure. When the 영 'young' [soul/spirit] has alot of anger and trauma which we refer to as 한 'han'...that spirit wont be able to pass into the spirit world peacefully. 
My grandmother was someone who was chosen and marked by the spirits, but she was unable to fulfill her destiny as a mudang. Instead she walked in the path of the Catholic faith, and despite being chosen by the gods... she began to mix the two up, and forming her own unique twist.

alt_text: Photo by Mudang Jenn 무당젠 on December 06, 2018.

description:
Beoseon [버선] 
When I toured Korea, my heart fluttered everytime I saw these. The traditional socks of Korea, shows the sorrows and joys of our Korean mothers and grandmothers. How you ask?
In traditional times, during holidays mothers and grandmothers would hand sew all the new clothing for their families to wear, such as new year. The woman would stay up all night long sewing and sewing tirelessly, so she may clothe her family in new garments.  When I first saw these at the marketplace,  I thought of my grandmother and it raised alot of bittersweet emotions. 
Even mudangs to this day, still wear beoseon's during kut ceremony/ritual. I sometimes do wear these beoseon myself. In older days when mudangs jumped during ceremonies,  they use to pour water on the wooden floors so the mudang wouldnt slip with the beoseon. The socks are slippery and throwing water down gave it grip. 
Growing up in NYC, I never thought of my ancestors,  my culture or traditions at all. And now, all I do is think of different ways of preserving what is sacred. Maybe because my ancestors are with me, I feel a stronger sense to protect these sacred traditions. Times are evolving and many are choosing modernism over traditions,  including mudangs. I choose to preserve my traditions, because I want to keep on weaving the story of our ancestors joy, sorrows and pains. I feel that keeping with my culture and traditions, is the physical storytelling of our ancestors. Someone told me that traditions like a fire that we keep adding wood to, to keep it alive. Beautiful indeed.

description:
Image taken from Google.
This is the god Daesin Halmoni (대신할머니). Daesin means Great Spirit, Halmoni means grandmother. This god helps with fortune telling, notice her bell rattles, rice, fan and old coins used for divination.
I remember my first vision, I was sitting on the couch at a friends house. I just closed my eyes for a split second to practice my breathwork meditation. Then like watching a movie, unable to move. I saw my grandmother, she appeared and she took my hand flew up towards the sky. I looked back as I left my family behind as heartbroken as I was, I willingly followed as she lead me to the sky. We flew up up up, high above the sky and clouds. Silently I paid my respects to all my family elders and said my goodbye as I was leaving. 
My grandmother took me on this woodland path, and there were fields of golden rice on both sides of a dirt road. The rice fields were shining brightly, and then she took me inside a cave where a huge figure sat in the dark. He was massively bigger than us, my grandmother immediately started to bow down but I was confused.  Who is he, or she? Looked like an ancient king of sorts.
Months later, that vision came true. In the October, I flew to korea leaving my family behind embarking on a sacred pilgrimage back to my ancestral land.  There while travelling in the countryside where vast golden fields of rice ready for harvest. In the mountains, I had my initiation where I am forever committed to my gods and deities.

description:
Can you feel the pain and trauma of this place. Do you see the pagoda in front of you, the 5 tiered stone granite pagoda. 
This pagoda was assumed to be built back in 1316, by a monk when the temple was being refurbished. 
The roof of the 2nd tier, 3rd tier, and the 4th contains bullet holes made during the Korean war (1950-1953). The original temple was built by Doseon a master who systematized Feng Shui theories in 887. Unfortunately the original temple was destroyed in the fire of during the Imjin war, the Japanese invasion of 1592. All of its buildings burned down except for this stone pagoda. 
In 1959, is when monks started to rebuild. .

description:

Even in my teen and early adult life, abuse was an ongoing theme. My grandmother was so obsessive with her faith that it blinded her. She became the wedge that divided me from my father. As she planted seeds of hate into his mind. She called me names like the devils child, satan and child of a whore all because she did not like my mother. She was not sane, but everyone in the family left her unchecked Including my father. 
I grew older and began to have relationships which would later echo the same abuse whether it was physicallyor mentally. Those relationship always went longer than it needed to, despite the abuse. I been in many circumstances of rape, and sexual abuse of adult men and male friends or colleagues. 
So despite the many trauma is my life, I rise with fervor. What they thought and tried to do to break me, only harden me. I went from shutting my mouth afraid to speak to setting my path ablaze. 
The values and characteristics that those around me failed miserably at of integrity,  respect and honor are my GREATEST assets. 
This isn't meant for pity,  this is meant for strength.  We rise through the ashes of our trauma, I survive and so can you if you are in an abusive situation. Those who abuse will chain you down to feed on you. If you know anyone in an abusive relationship,  abusive family. Do not turn your cheek. Seek help, guidance...there are many resources now than ever. Simply put. There is no fucking excuse for abuse. .
Now I have 2 young boys of my own, and super fucking supportive partner in all I do.  My own pain, life sufferings has molded and shaped me to become the healer I am, the mudang I am.

description:
I had the pleasure and honor of being asked by the editor of Sacred Hoops Magazine to write about muism and my personal journey into the world of mugyo. 
Korean shamanism mugyo isnt well known, as most mudang manshin shamans dont frequently service outside of their own culture. When I first felt my own calling, Ive thought about travelling into South America to meet with a shaman to learn, but more and more I felt pulled into my ancestral culture. I feel different, like a bridge to fill the gap between my two culture being American and Korean. 
Korean shamanism scared the shit out of me, it seemed more abrasive and harsher than other cultures. Shamans dancing on giant butcher knives, performing exorcism and acting all crazy gave me so much fear. But despite my fear, I was fated to meet an amazing teacher who held my hand and believed in my gifts. I forever indebted to my spirit mother, for she gave me a new life and breath in my lungs. 
Im still debating if I should write an article, its very humbling and at the same time stressful as I am sure not many articles are written about mugyo muism. This is my chance to voice my cultural heritage, and Im sure this opportunity isnt just a coincidence...

description:
Part (2/2) 
A soft glow of light walked towards us. I couldn't see through my tears until she was standing right in front of me. Her hair was was twisted in double loops, I call it '토끼 머리' means rabbit hair. Her garment was so seamless looked like flowing waters. 
She took the black lump from the Jangun hands, and covered it with her own. She began to glow as she seemed to put her energy into the black ball. She put her hands in front of me, and slowly uncovered the ball. It was no longer black, instead looked like a orb full of intense bright colors of the rainbow.
I did not know what it meant at the time, as no words were spoken only gestures. She seemed very pleased as she showed joy in the ball. She gave the colored orb back to 장군 Jangun. He took the orb, and pierced my heart again with his sword. He placed it back. 
No words were spoken but the visions spoke a thousand words. The message was clear, I knew I was given a gift. It ignited a colorful passion within me, the energy of the gods was alive in my heart and body. I felt renewed, reawakened. 
We packed our bags and belongings, but my tears were still flowing. Spirit mom told me to walk around the mountain path, to let the 기 energy flow in my heart. My group left me behind to give me privacy,  and instead I sobbed my way down.
It wasn't until in the early sunrise, did I see the shrine. My heart was literally going to burst, as I came across the shrine for the Heaven Maiden 선녀 Seonyo. I lit a candle and incense,  I began to bow and pray because of the overwhelming gratitude that was pouring out of me. This was an affirmation that what I saw was right, especially to see the shrine for 선녀 after my vision. I made a vow right then and there, to refortify and renew my promise to my spirits and path. I hope to light my path with blazing colors bringing hope and healing.

description:
Happy 칠성날 (Chil-seong day)
Chil-seong is the Korean shamanic Heavenly deity/gods of longevity specifically for the wellbeing of children. It also literally means 7 stars, referencing the 7 brightest star of the Great Bear constellation also known as the Big Dipper.
Although Chil-seong is depicted as 7 individual but treated as one deity. Chil-seong the shamanic deity later absorbed into Buddhism, Taoism, etc. Because Chil-seong is very prominent, it is easier to find them at a Buddhist temple than other shamanic gods/deities.
Today is a day of Chil-seong (칠성), usually any  family with children would visit the mudang, ask to be included in the Chil-seong ceremony. Each child name is written on a long piece of white cloth to represent their life line. We put up offerings, we drum and pray for those children. Ask for the heavenly Chil-seong god to hear our prayers, our songs. That each child whom we pray for grows big, healthy and strong. 
칠성 Chil-seong is one of the oldest worship god/deity in the Korean shamanism.

To protect the families and their children the names have been blurred out

description:
Samsin [삼신], the grandmother deity known as the goddess of children and/or childbearing. She is a shamanic deity and a house spirit that watches, protects and guides all children until the age of 7 years. 
Most household have a "danji" [earthen pot deity shrine] within the "warmest part of the home" as the location of Samsin.  When a child is born, it is customary to set up an offering table of seaweed soup [miyuk gook], steamed rice, water, and 3 vegetable sides. When the child hits various milestones like 100th day and 1 year birthday, an offering table is set for Samsin to give gratitude and ask for blessings. "Sam" [pronounced sahm] means three, "Sin" [pronounced shin] means god or deity. Samsin is a triple goddess treated as one deity. She is also a household deity [gasin] protecting the inner quarters of the home. Samsin is also know as Jesuk or Jesok, depicted as the 3 Buddhist. 
All children enter this world upon with the blessing of Samsin, but their fate lifeline is determined by  Chilseong, the deity of the seven stars [big dipper constellation]
With the introduction of buddhism in the early 4th century, most shamanic origin myth and stories were re-written with the influence of the Male monks. Samsin is originally 3 goddess but rewritten as 3 Male bodhisattva of fate, luck and mercy. Before then most of the shamanic stories, and myths were passed down orally without any written accounts.  #koreanshamanism #koreanshaman #shaman #shamanism #witch #intuitive #goddess #clairvoyance #childbirth #blessings  #fate #offerings #deities #gratitude #healing #esoteric #shrine #altar #sacredspace #witchythings #witchesofinstagram #gratitude #spiritguides #뉴욕무당 #미국무당 #기도 #무당 #무속인 #애동제자 #감사합니다 #기도 #삼신
